title: Classification of bipartite observables II: NIP observables and the Todorcevic trichotomy
abstract: A bipartite observable is stable when its idealized responses are continuous. We show that it is NIP exactly when they are of the first Baire class. They then form a Rosenthal compactum, and the dividing lines of Shelah in model theory, together with the classification of Rosenthal compacta of Todorčević, acquire a physical meaning. For observables, mixtures of states make every hereditarily separable compactum of idealized responses metrizable, and the Todorčević trichotomy becomes a classification into three classes. Each class contains a physical order: the comparison of photon numbers, the comparison of positions, and the causal order of spacetime, whose idealized responses are not first countable because a light cone can shrink to a point; the comparison of two phases on a circle joins it there. Each of the seven minimal families of the heptachotomy, which Argyros, Dodos and Kanellopoulos extracted from the methods of Todorčević, is realized by a tree of preparations of photons, of a particle in a box, or of a spin chain read by a probe; the spin chain also shows that NIP, unlike its uniform version, is not symmetric between the two parties. Finally, for the Ising model in a transverse field we show that, in the ordered phase, the responses of the two pure phases form split pairs whose midpoints, the responses of the symmetric state, form an uncountable discrete set; the proof uses a Lee--Yang theorem for this model.
summary: This paper classifies bipartite quantum observables by mapping their idealized response functions onto abstract mathematical structures derived from model theory and descriptive set theory. It establishes that physical properties like stability correspond to specific mathematical regularity conditions (e.g., being of the first Baire class). The work provides a powerful, abstract framework for understanding the limitations and structure of quantum measurements.
main_problem: The paper classifies bipartite quantum observables by linking their mathematical properties (like the NIP condition) to topological and set-theoretic structures (Todorčević trichotomy). It aims to establish a rigorous dictionary between abstract model theory and physical measurements.
main_result: The classification shows that observables fall into distinct mathematical classes (related to the Todorčević trichotomy), with specific physical examples like photon number comparison belonging to certain NIP levels.
method: The analysis heavily employs advanced mathematical tools, including model theory (NIP property, Shelah's dividing lines) and descriptive set theory (Rosenthal compacta, Todorčević trichotomy).
model_or_system: The study focuses on bipartite observables measured on two independent quantum systems. Specific models analyzed include the Ising model in a transverse field, photon number comparisons, and position/causal order comparisons.
key_observables: Idealized responses of observables, stability, NIP property, superfluid weight ($D_s$), and Drude weight ($D$).
important_parameters: The analysis depends on the order of limits when calculating expectation values (e.g., $\lim_{m	o 0} \lim_{V	o\infty}$ vs. $\lim_{V	o\infty} \lim_{m	o 0}$), and the gap structure of excitations.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mathematical validity of idealized preparations (limits) and specific assumptions (S1) and (S2) regarding spectral representations.
figures_summary: Figures map the classification space, showing how physical systems realize the seven minimal families derived from the Todorčević trichotomy.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining stability and the NIP property for observables, relating these to the structure of their idealized response sets (Rosenthal compacta), and then mapping this structure onto the known classification schemes from model theory (Todorčević trichotomy).
why_interesting: It provides a deep, abstract framework for understanding when quantum measurements are well-behaved (stable/NIP) by connecting quantum information diagnostics to fundamental results in set theory and model theory.
